Section 1 of 5

Why Freeze?

Free. Separate. Reversible. A credit freeze restricts access to a credit report, making many new-account fraud attempts harder. Anyone can request one, even before identity theft occurs. Freeze all three major bureaus separately.

By the end, you can explain what a freeze protects, find the three official freeze pages, plan a short thaw, and compare alerts with monitoring.

Why freeze?

A thief may use exposed identifying information to apply for credit. Restricting access to your reports adds a barrier. A freeze does not lower your credit score or stop you using existing credit cards.

What remains your job?

A freeze does not stop charges on existing accounts, account takeover, medical or tax identity theft, or scams that persuade you to send money. It does not repair report errors or add a fraud alert automatically.

Expect a little planning

Your own new-credit application may need a temporary lift. Ask before rental, employment, insurance, phone, or utility checks whether a lift is needed. Some permitted access, including certain existing-creditor reviews, continues during a freeze.

Four useful words

Bureau
A company that maintains credit reports.
Freeze
A free restriction on access for new credit, with legal protections.
Thaw
A temporary lift for a chosen time window.
Refreeze
Restoring the restriction after access is no longer needed.

Place a Freeze

Practice only: No activity here freezes real credit. Do not enter Social Security numbers, birth dates, addresses, passwords, or confirmation codes. This guide has no fields for that information. Activity progress stays only in this open page.

Prepare privately

Use a trusted device and connection. Official bureaus need identity verification, which may include your name, address history, date of birth, and Social Security number. Supply it only through a verified bureau channel. Use unique passwords and multi-factor authentication when offered. Keep confirmations and recovery details in a password manager or another secure place.

Use each official page below. Create or sign in to the free account, find security freeze, submit the request, and verify the status says frozen. A paid plan, trial, credit score product, or credit lock is not required. Screen labels can change.

Thaw & Refreeze

  1. Ask the lender which bureau or bureaus it needs and when.
  2. Go directly to those official bureau accounts or call their verified numbers.
  3. Select a temporary lift and a start and end date covering the check. Save the confirmation privately.
  4. Confirm the report is available before the lender checks it. Online/phone lifts must occur within one hour; mailed lifts within three business days after receipt. Leave time for verification or access problems.
  5. At the end of a scheduled lift, the freeze returns. Check each affected bureau’s status. If you removed the freeze permanently instead, place a new free freeze yourself.

Keep unaffected bureaus frozen. If the lender needs another bureau later, lift that one too. Choose a short window that still covers the legitimate check.

Practice a short access window

Fictional example: A lender needs only Experian on Tuesday. All three fictional reports begin frozen. Advance through the sequence; this does not use real dates or contact a bureau.

Step 1 of 4

Before Tuesday: Equifax frozen; Experian frozen; TransUnion frozen.

Temporary versus permanent: A scheduled thaw has an end. Permanent removal stays open until you request a new freeze. Neither action costs money.

USAGov: lifting a freeze (opens in new tab). Return to the bureau links in the Freeze tab to manage real requests.

Alerts & Monitoring

A freeze restricts report access. A fraud alert prompts identity checks. Monitoring notifies you about selected changes. These tools can work together, but none prevents every kind of identity theft.

Compare what each tool does and costs
ToolPurpose and limitsCost / action
Credit freezeRestricts access for new credit; does not protect existing account transactions.Free to place, lift, and replace. Contact all three bureaus separately.
Fraud alertAsks lenders to verify identity; report access remains available. Can coexist with freezes.Free. Contact one major bureau; it must notify the other two.
Credit monitoringDetects selected report changes. Check whether coverage includes one, two, or all three bureaus and how often. It does not block applications or watch every bank withdrawal.Some free services or benefits; other plans charge monthly or annually.
Identity monitoringLooks for information in selected databases or online sources. A “dark web” scan cannot prove your identity is safe or erase all stolen information. Coverage varies.May be bundled with paid plans or available as a benefit. No universal price.
Credit lockA contractual bureau product; terms and availability vary. It differs from a legally regulated security freeze.May be free or part of a paid plan. Not necessary to obtain a freeze.

Compare what each tool does and costs

Credit freeze

Purpose and limits
Restricts access for new credit; does not protect existing account transactions.
Cost / action
Free to place, lift, and replace. Contact all three bureaus separately.

Fraud alert

Purpose and limits
Asks lenders to verify identity; report access remains available. Can coexist with freezes.
Cost / action
Free. Contact one major bureau; it must notify the other two.

Credit monitoring

Purpose and limits
Detects selected report changes. Check whether coverage includes one, two, or all three bureaus and how often. It does not block applications or watch every bank withdrawal.
Cost / action
Some free services or benefits; other plans charge monthly or annually.

Identity monitoring

Purpose and limits
Looks for information in selected databases or online sources. A “dark web” scan cannot prove your identity is safe or erase all stolen information. Coverage varies.
Cost / action
May be bundled with paid plans or available as a benefit. No universal price.

Credit lock

Purpose and limits
A contractual bureau product; terms and availability vary. It differs from a legally regulated security freeze.
Cost / action
May be free or part of a paid plan. Not necessary to obtain a freeze.

Choose the right fraud alert

  • Initial: If you suspect identity theft; lasts one year and can be renewed.
  • Extended: For identity-theft victims with an FTC identity theft report or police report; lasts seven years.
  • Active duty: For active duty servicemembers; lasts one year and can be renewed for the deployment.

FTC: alert eligibility, duration, and bureau contacts (opens in new tab)

A safe way to compare monitoring

  1. Start with free freezes, account transaction alerts, and regular report reviews at AnnualCreditReport.com (opens in new tab). You can read your own reports while frozen.
  2. Check existing bank, employer, insurance, or verified breach-notice benefits before paying. Verify an offer independently; do not enroll through an unexpected message.
  3. Read the full renewal price, trial expiry, cancellation process, bureau coverage, alert frequency, privacy policy, and what data is collected. Compare the annual total, not just a promotional monthly rate.
  4. Ask what recovery assistance actually does. Insurance has limits, exclusions, and possibly a deductible; it does not guarantee repayment of stolen funds. Review the policy rather than relying on an advertised coverage maximum.

Monitoring is detection, often after activity appears. Keep checking bank and retirement accounts and Medicare statements; monitoring may miss tax or benefit fraud. Never give a caller your password, verification code, or remote access to “activate protection.”

Illustrative cost comparison (not a current product offer)

A fictional plan at $15 per month costs $180 per year; a fictional $25 plan costs $300. A higher price alone does not demonstrate better coverage. Free freezes remain available with either plan or with no subscription.

Safety & Check

When something looks wrong

Pause and end unexpected contact. Verify through a known number or official website. If money was sent, contact the bank or payment provider promptly. For a suspicious new account, contact the company and use IdentityTheft.gov (opens in new tab) for an FTC recovery plan. Report scams at ReportFraud.ftc.gov (opens in new tab). Save evidence privately.

From the seniors’ fraud handout: pressure, secrecy, unusual payment requests, and requests for codes are reasons to stop and verify. A “grandchild in trouble” or fake tech-support emergency still needs independent verification even when your credit is frozen.
